submission.natural_language_explanation: N830+ detects the release event of a product, media work, service or venue - the moment it is brought into public availability or circulation by a producer, retailer or presenter - firing hardest on the event word itself ('ship' 3.37, 'opening' 3.05, 'launched' 2.92, 'launch' 2.81, 'released' 2.79, 'available' 2.72, 'release' 2.69, 'opened' 2.34) and secondarily on the availability-timing words that state or anticipate it ('not yet' 1.8-2.3, 'due for release' 1.78, 'slated', 'soon', 'coming', 'ready'). It is retrospective rather than lookahead (58% of input attribution is on the event token, replacement effect there 0.98-1.00, and zero-ablating the pole leaves next-token predictions diffuse, not concentrated on any upcoming token), and it is context-gated, not token-gated: the same token stays near zero when the preceding subject is not a producer/venue committing the act ('the door opened' 0.00 vs 'the store opened' 1.81; 'the police released the hostage' 0.00 vs 'the studio will release' 2.41; 'NASA will launch the rocket' 0.12; 'began/started/finished/published/issued' all <0.4), while consumer-product nouns and trade vocabulary ('new phone' 1.74, 'crossover SUV' 1.19, 'cost' 1.20, 'popular' 1.03, 'box office' 2.5-3.0) give a weaker secondary rise and generic 'not yet'/'due' temporals a weaker leftover (~1.0-1.4).

The old bonded warehouse on the eastern edge of the county stood empty for the better part of a decade, its brick walls stained dark by a century of coal smoke and its interior divided into long aisles of steel racks. When the Henderson family bought the property in 2014 they had no particular plan for it. The building came with the surrounding pasture, and the pasture came with a spring that ran cold and clear all year, and it was the spring that eventually decided the matter. Water, as every distiller will tell you, is the part of the process you cannot fix later.

The first mash went into the still in the autumn of 2015, using barley grown on the neighbouring farm and malted a few miles down the valley. The family hired a former cooper named Alice Ruiz to manage the floor, and she brought with her a set of practices that had fallen out of fashion: open fermentation, long and slow, and a stubborn refusal to chill-filter. The first barrels were laid down in the low aisles closest to the north wall, where the temperature swings least between summer and winter, and where the angel's share, according to Ruiz, is at its gentlest.

For the first few years almost nothing came out of the warehouse. A small amount of unaged spirit was sold at the farm gate, mostly to neighbours, and a handful of barrels were traded with a distillery on the other side of the county in exchange for the use of its bottling line. The family planted a hedgerow of sloe and elder along the access road, partly as a windbreak and partly, they admitted later, because it looked better in photographs than a gravel yard.

The turning point came in 2019, when a buyer for a regional grocery chain tasted a sample from cask 118 and asked whether there might be enough to supply a dozen stores. There was not, not that year, and Ruiz said so plainly. But the question changed how the family thought about the warehouse. They stopped treating the barrels as a hobby and started treating them as inventory. Two more stills were ordered. A second rickhouse went up behind the first, clad in the same dark brick so that from the road the two buildings read as one.

The spirit itself has changed with the years, as it always does. The earliest casks show more cereal and less fruit than the later ones; the middle years, when the barley came from a wetter harvest, are rounder and a shade sweeter. Ruiz keeps a notebook of every fill and every dump, and she can tell you, from the number alone, which field the grain came from and how long the wash sat before it went into the still.

Tasting notes for the twelve-year-old, written by Ruiz last month, describe honeysuckle and damp stone on the nose, a palate of baked apple and a faint salinity, and a finish that lingers longer than the price suggests it should. The distillery will release the first six hundred bottles of the twelve-year-old at the visitor centre on Saturday, October 12, with a two-bottle limit per customer and the remainder going on sale through the distillery's website the following Monday.

The family expects the bottling to sell out within a day. They have been wrong about this before, and Ruiz, for one, would not mind being wrong again.
